opus-5.5.text:
I think the key distinction is about where the bottleneck sits. In math, and to a large extent in theoretical physics, the whole loop can happen in your head, or now inside a computer. You have an idea, you work through the consequences, and you can check whether the reasoning holds up without ever touching the physical world. A proof is either correct or it isn't, and increasingly we can even verify that formally. So if you have a system that's good at reasoning, it can generate, test, and refine ideas at the speed of compute. There's no wet lab in the loop.

Physics is a little more nuanced because ultimately it is an empirical science. But a huge amount of progress in theoretical physics comes from taking known principles, symmetries, and mathematical structures and pushing them further. When I was doing research, much of the day-to-day work was calculation and consistency checking. That's exactly the kind of thing that should be very amenable to AI as these models get better at long chains of reasoning.

Biology is different. It's messy in a way that doesn't compress nicely into a small set of principles. There's evolutionary history baked into everything, a lot of contingency, and enormous complexity across scales, from molecules to cells to organisms. Very often you just can't reason your way to the answer. You have to run the experiment, and experiments are slow, expensive, and noisy. So even a superhumanly smart model is bottlenecked by how fast you can collect data from the real world.

There's also the question of training signal. In math you have clean, verifiable feedback: did the proof go through or not? That's great for reinforcement learning. In biology the feedback is delayed, partial, and often ambiguous, which makes it much harder to set up that tight improvement loop.

So I'd put it this way: math and physics are domains where intelligence itself is the main constraint, so improving intelligence translates pretty directly into progress. In biology intelligence helps a lot, but it's not the only constraint, and the world pushes back. That doesn't mean AI won't transform biology. I think it will. But I'd expect the first really striking AI-driven breakthroughs to show up in math and theoretical physics, simply because there's less friction between thinking and knowing.

r001.rationale: It says mathematical reasoning can be worked through and checked without touching the physical world.

r002.rationale: It describes math as computer-based and self-contained, but does not connect that feature to text generation or the setting in which language models operate.

r003.rationale: It contrasts clean mathematical feedback with biology’s delayed, partial feedback and says real-world data collection is slow, making biology harder to train on.

r004.rationale: It says biology requires experiments, but does not argue that a self-sustaining AI biologist would need a means to carry them out.

r005.rationale: It explains that biology’s dependence on slow, noisy physical experiments makes progress harder than in domains where thinking and checking can happen without the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that math and physics are the domains where the loop between thinking and checking is almost entirely closed inside the head, or inside the computer. If I want to know whether a proof is right, I don't need to go anywhere. I don't need to wait for anything. I can sit down and verify it, or better yet, hand it to a formal system like Lean and get a yes or no. That makes it a nearly perfect environment for a model to learn in, because you can generate an enormous amount of reasoning and get crisp feedback on all of it. The reward signal is clean and it's cheap. That's exactly the regime where reinforcement learning on these models has worked really well.

Physics is a little messier than math, but a surprising amount of theoretical physics behaves the same way. You have a tight formal structure, a set of equations, and you're asking whether a derivation holds or whether a calculation comes out consistent. Even where you ultimately need an experiment, a lot of the intellectual work happens before that, in a space where you can check yourself. And I say that as someone who came up as a theoretical physicist, so I'm maybe biased about how much of it is pencil and paper, but a lot of it really is.

Biology is different in kind, not just degree. The ground truth lives in the world, in cells and organisms, and getting it out is slow, expensive, and noisy. If a model has a hypothesis about a protein or a pathway, there's no equivalent of running the proof checker. Someone has to do the experiment, that takes days or weeks, and even then the result has error bars and confounders. So the number of times you can close the loop is tiny compared to math, and each iteration gives you a fuzzier signal. On top of that, our theoretical understanding is just thinner. In physics, if you understand the principles, you can often predict the answer. In biology, the system is the product of billions of years of contingent evolution, and there aren't many principles compact enough that a model could reason from them to a confident prediction without touching reality.

So it's not that biology is harder to think about. It's that it's harder to practice at. These models get good at what they can repeat and get graded on millions of times. Math and physics let you do that today. For biology, you'd need the lab itself to become fast and automated enough to be part of the training loop, and that's really a robotics and infrastructure problem as much as an AI problem. I think it will happen, but it puts biology a few steps behind on the curve, and that gap tells you something about where we should expect the first really dramatic scientific contributions from AI to show up.

r001.rationale: It says a proof can be checked without going anywhere or waiting, including by a formal system, so much of mathematics needs no physical experiment.

r002.rationale: It connects mathematics’ self-contained checks to model training and generated reasoning, but never connects that character to the text-generation setting of language models.

r003.rationale: It explains that biology’s ground truth requires slow, costly, noisy experiments, making feedback and training iterations scarce and less reliable than in self-contained domains.

r004.rationale: It says biology’s training loop would require the lab itself to become fast and automated, identifying physical experimentation as necessary for an AI biologist.

r005.rationale: It argues that biology is harder for AI because its ground truth is in the physical world and experiments are slow, expensive, and noisy.

astra-6.text:
I think “easy” is relative here. Mathematics and physics can be extraordinarily hard, but they have a structure that’s very helpful for AI. In mathematics, you can specify a problem precisely, and there’s often a way to check whether an answer is correct. In physics, we look for relatively simple laws that explain a huge range of observations. That gives you strong constraints on what a good answer can look like.

Biology is much messier. You’re dealing with systems shaped by evolution, with all sorts of historical contingencies and interactions across scales. Understanding a molecule doesn’t automatically tell you how a cell will behave, let alone an organism. And the measurements are often noisy and incomplete.

So the distinction isn’t that biology somehow defies computation. It’s that the problem is harder to specify, the relevant information is harder to collect, and checking your prediction may require an expensive experiment. In mathematics, you might verify a proof. In biology, you may have to go back to the lab.

r001.rationale: It says a mathematical proof may be verified, but does not explain that much of mathematics can be pursued without physical-world experiments.

r002.rationale: It does not connect mathematics’ self-contained character to language models or text generation.

r003.rationale: It mentions that biological information is difficult to collect, but does not identify suitable training data as a difficulty that grows when tasks move beyond self-contained domains.

r004.rationale: It says checking a biological prediction may require going back to the lab, but does not argue that a self-sustaining AI biologist needs a means to conduct physical experiments.

r005.rationale: It notes that biological predictions may require expensive experiments, but does not state the general claim that greater dependence on physical-world interaction makes a domain harder for AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics and physics have a tremendous advantage: you can often state the rules precisely, and you have a clear way to check whether an answer is right. In mathematics, that might be a proof. In physics, you often have a small set of equations that captures a remarkably wide range of phenomena. That gives an AI a lot of structure to work with.

Biology is much messier. You’re dealing with systems shaped by evolution, with many interacting components, and the details of the context can completely change the outcome. A result in one cell type might not hold in another. Even measuring what’s happening can be difficult, and testing a hypothesis may require an expensive experiment that takes weeks or months.

So “easy” is relative. Mathematics and physics can be extremely hard, but they often offer cleaner problems and better feedback. In biology, figuring out what the right question is—and what evidence would actually answer it—is a substantial part of the challenge.

r001.rationale: It identifies mathematical proofs as a way to check answers, conveying that mathematics can be pursued without physical experiments.

r002.rationale: It does not connect mathematics’ self-contained character to language models’ text-generation setting.

r003.rationale: It mentions difficult experiments in biology but says nothing about obtaining suitable training data.

r004.rationale: It notes that biological hypotheses may require experiments, but does not say a self-sustaining AI biologist would need a way to conduct them.

r005.rationale: It contrasts mathematical proofs with costly biological experiments, but does not clearly state that greater dependence on physical-world interaction makes a domain harder for AI.
